title: Grilled Polenta Wedges
subtitle: set polenta sliced and grilled until crisp at the edges
excerpt: Grilled polenta wedges start with a basic soft polenta poured into a tray and left to set firm. The slices are then grilled or fried until the outside is crisp and golden while the inside stays creamy. Serves 4 as a side.
sourceNotes: The practice of pouring soft polenta into a tray or onto a board, allowing it to set firm, and then slicing and grilling or frying it is documented throughout northern Italian cooking. Pellegrino Artusi, La scienza in cucina (1891, public domain in Italy), mentions the practice of allowing leftover polenta to firm and then grilling it as a practical use of surplus. Polenta fritta and polenta grigliata are standard preparations in trattorie throughout Lombardy, Veneto, and Piedmont, particularly as a starchy accompaniment to braised meats, wild mushrooms, or roasted vegetables.

recipe.batchNotes: Make double the polenta and refrigerate the second batch for up to 3 days. Slice and grill as needed.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: The set polenta can be made up to 3 days ahead and kept refrigerated. Grill to order.

glossaryTerms.definition: Soft polenta poured into a tray and left to cool and firm completely. Once set, it holds its shape when sliced and can be grilled, fried, or baked. Polenta sets more firmly as it cools; refrigerating for an hour or overnight makes it very easy to slice cleanly.

content.text: Grilled polenta wedges solve the leftover polenta problem while also being a good dish in their own right. Soft polenta poured into an oiled tray, left to set firm, then sliced into wedges and grilled until the outside is crisp and golden. The inside stays soft and creamy; the outside crisps like toast. They pair well with mushrooms, braised greens, or any slow-cooked sauce.

Polenta must be cooled completely before slicing, preferably for an hour at room temperature or overnight in the fridge. Warm polenta sticks to the knife and falls apart. Cold, firm polenta slices cleanly and holds its shape on the grill.

Oil a 20 cm x 30 cm tray or baking dish. Bring {{water}} of water to the boil with {{salt-table}} of salt. Whisk in {{polenta-coarse}} of polenta in a thin stream. Reduce heat and cook according to the packet (5 minutes for instant; 35 minutes for coarse), stirring frequently, until thick and smooth. Stir in rosemary if using.
Pour the polenta into the prepared tray and spread level to about 2 cm thick. Leave to cool at room temperature for 1 hour, or refrigerate for up to 3 days.
out onto a board. Cut into wedges, rectangles, or thick slices. Brush all over with {{olive-oil}} of olive oil.

Heat a griddle pan, grill pan, or non-stick frying pan over a high heat. Cook the polenta slices for 3 to 4 minutes per side without moving them, until grid marks form and the exterior is golden and crisp. Alternatively, brush with oil and grill under a hot oven grill for 4 to 5 minutes per side.
Serve immediately. Finish with flaked sea salt if wanted.

items.symptom: Polenta sticks to the grill pan and breaks
items.cause: Not cooled long enough, or pan not hot enough
items.fix: The polenta must be fully cold and firm. The pan must be very hot and well-oiled. Do not move the slices until they naturally release.

items.cause: Pan not hot enough, or polenta too wet
items.fix: Use high heat and let the slices sit undisturbed. A soft polenta base (too much water) will not crisp well; the polenta for setting should be made with slightly less liquid than for serving soft.

content.text: Grilled polenta appears in mountain trattorie across northern Italy as a side dish alongside mushrooms, braised boar, or grilled sausage. It began as a way of using leftover cold polenta: the Italian habit of not wasting food applied to the staple grain of the Alps. As a dish in its own right, it is valued for the contrast between the crisp outside and the creamy inside, which soft polenta cannot give. It is now common on restaurant menus throughout northern Italy.
